---
title: "Quiz: measuring surfaces"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Meshes are closed and oriented with outward normals unless said otherwise.

---

**Q1.** Why must a mesh be closed to compute its volume by summing signed tetrahedra?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What cancels in the sum?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The tetrahedra from the origin to the triangles overlap; only for a closed surface do the parts outside the object cancel between the near and far side, leaving exactly the enclosed volume. With a hole, part of the boundary is missing and the sum depends on where the origin is.
:::

---

**Q2.** A sphere is digitised at a very fine resolution. Which estimate is good and which is bad: volume from the voxel count, area from the exposed voxel faces?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Does a staircase get closer to a slope when its steps get smaller?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The voxel count converges to the true volume. The face count stays about 1.5 times the true area at any resolution: smaller steps, but the same total length of steps per unit of slope.
:::

---

**Q3.** A mesh has $V = 1000$, $E = 3000$, $F = 2000$. What is $\chi$, and what could the surface be?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\chi = V - E + F$; a closed surface with $g$ holes has $\chi = 2 - 2g$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\chi = 0$: for example one torus (one hole), or one sphere ($+2$) plus a surface with two holes ($-2$). Count the components to tell.
:::

---

**Q4.** Two objects have the same true volume. Object A is large with sharp edges, object B small and blurred. Which one's measured volume depends more on $c$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How far does the surface move when $c$ changes a little?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
B. A blurred edge has a small gradient, so a small change of $c$ moves the surface a long way, and a small object has a large fraction of its volume near the surface. A's volume-against-$c$ curve has a plateau; B's is steep.
:::

---

**Q5.** You smooth a mesh with many iterations of Laplacian smoothing. What happens to its volume, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where is the mean of a vertex's neighbours on a convex surface?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It shrinks. On a convex surface the mean of a vertex's neighbours lies inside the surface, so every step moves the vertices inwards; repeated, the whole mesh contracts (a sphere shrinks towards a point).
:::

---

**Q6.** A confocal stack has $\Delta z = 3\Delta x$. The volume of a cell is computed from a mesh whose vertices were placed with $\Delta z = \Delta x$. By what factor is the volume wrong?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Only one coordinate is scaled.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
All $z$ coordinates are 3 times too small, so the volume is 3 times too small (a factor $1/3$).
:::

---

**Q7.** Why does a mesh from a binary mask (0/1) at $c = 0.5$ look terraced, and why does this inflate its area?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where on each edge does the vertex go?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
All edge values are 1 and 0, so every vertex is at an edge midpoint: the vertices follow the voxel staircase instead of the smooth boundary. The steps add area, like voxel faces but less (about 8 % for a sphere), at any resolution.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Compute the signed volume $\tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot(\mathbf b\times\mathbf c)$ of the tetrahedron with $\mathbf a = (1, 0, 0)$, $\mathbf b = (0, 1, 0)$, $\mathbf c = (0, 0, 1)$ and the origin. What happens if you swap $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
$\mathbf b\times\mathbf c$ for two unit axis vectors.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$\mathbf b\times\mathbf c = (1, 0, 0)$, so $\tfrac16\,\mathbf a\cdot(1, 0, 0) = \tfrac16$. Swapping $\mathbf b$ and $\mathbf c$ reverses the orientation: $-\tfrac16$.
:::
